title: Realign — Desk Posture Reset
subtitle: Counter forward-rounded, desk-driven posture
coaching_note: This is corrective work, not a hard workout — the goal is waking up muscles that have gone quiet from sitting, not fatiguing them. If you spend most of your day at a desk, this is worth two sessions a week minimum, not just when something already hurts.

phases.name: Release
phases.coaching_note: Chest and hip flexors get tight from sitting — release those first so the activation work below actually sticks.

exercises.name: Doorway Chest Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Forearm on the doorframe at shoulder height, lean your body through the doorway until you feel the stretch across your chest.
exercises.why: Tight pecs pull the shoulders forward and down — this is the single biggest driver of rounded desk posture.

exercises.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.form_cue: Back knee down, tuck your tailbone under first, then gently drive your hips forward.
exercises.why: Hours of hip flexion at a desk shortens these muscles, which tilts the pelvis forward and loads the lower back.

phases.name: Activation
phases.coaching_note: These muscles have usually gone quiet, not weak — expect them to feel awkward at first. That feeling fades in a few sessions.

exercises.name: Band Pull-Apart
exercises.form_cue: Arms straight, pull the band apart to touch your chest, squeeze your shoulder blades hard at the end range.
exercises.why: Directly activates the mid-trapezius and rhomboids — the muscles that pull your shoulders back out of a rounded position.

exercises.name: Band Y-Raise
exercises.form_cue: Slight forward lean, arms form a Y at about 45 degrees, thumbs up, raise to shoulder height only.
exercises.why: Targets the lower trapezius specifically — the piece that's almost always the weakest link in rounded shoulder posture.

exercises.name: Prone Cobra
exercises.form_cue: Face down, arms at your sides, lift your chest and squeeze your shoulder blades together and down, thumbs point up.
exercises.why: Builds endurance in the upper back extensors that fight gravity all day to keep you upright — bodyweight but genuinely hard when done right.

exercises.name: Chin Tuck
exercises.form_cue: Sitting tall, glide your head straight back like making a double chin, don't tilt up or down.
exercises.why: Directly retrains forward head posture — one of the most common and least-addressed desk postural faults.

exercises.name: Thread the Needle
exercises.form_cue: On all fours, thread one arm under your body and through, rotating your upper back, then unwind and reach it up toward the ceiling.
exercises.why: Restores thoracic rotation that the activation work needs in order to hold — mobility and strength work together here.

exercises.name: Standing Forward Fold
exercises.form_cue: Soft knees, let your head and arms hang, breathe slow into your lower back.
exercises.why: Decompresses the spine before you're done — a good close for any session that leaned on the upper back.

progression_notes: Once band pull-aparts and Y-raises feel easy at this volume, move to a heavier band rather than more reps — this work should stay in a low-fatigue, high-quality range.
